Discharge Summary:  
Patient Information: [redacted] (Female, DOB: [redacted], Hospital ID: [redacted]) was admitted with chronic anicteric cholestasis and worsening cough. Diagnosed with chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS) complicating sarcoidosis, confirmed via liver, gastric, and skin biopsies. Received oral prednisolone and warfarin anticoagulation. Discharged in stable condition with instructions to continue medication and attend follow-up appointments. Key findings include elevated cholestatic enzymes, anemia, hepatomegaly, and imaging evidence of BCS. No other conditions identified.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient [Name], Female, 26 years old, admitted in 2011 with profound hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness. Audiometry revealed a 37-dB hearing loss in left ear (70% speech discrimination), with right ear normal pure tone audiometry. Radiological findings included a 4 mm diameter CPA mass in the left internal auditory canal, consistent with a lipoma. Discharged with follow-up imaging and routine otolaryngology follow-up.

Discharge Summary:  
A 57-year-old male with extensive tobacco use, nonischemic cardiomyopathy, and ECOG PS 3 was admitted for mechanical cardiac support with a left ventricular assist device (LVAD) due to severe heart failure after initial evaluation. Three months post-surgery, mediastinal widening was noted, and CT scans showed mediastinal lymphadenopathy without disease outside the chest. Mediastinoscopy confirmed consistent SCLC. The patient was removed from cardiac transplant consideration, started chemotherapy (carboplatin and IV etoposide), and elected not to receive further treatment. Complications included cellulitis, neutropenic fevers, pseudomonal infection, prolonged nausea, and renal issues, which were managed with prolonged IV antibiotics. While renal function remained normal, left-sided pleural effusion and edema worsened the outcome, leading to hospice care and discharge. The patient passed away 6 months post-chemotherapy.

Admission Date: [Date]  
Discharge Date: [Date]  

Patient Name: [Patient Name]  Age: 72  Sex: Female  
Admitted to hospital for carcinoma of the right breast with enlarged axillary lymph nodes. Given neoadjuvant systemic therapy with anastrozole (Arimidex®) and abemaciclib (Verzenio®), followed by adjuvant 3D conformal radiotherapy (RTX) of the right breast and supraclavicular region. Post-RTX, a 2cm cutis edema and inflammatory changes occurred, leading to a targeted punch biopsy. Histology showed no malignant tumor, but fibrosis and dermal thickening. Diagnosed with postradiogenic circumscribed scleroderma 20 months post-RTX. Patient declined systemic therapies but used topical steroids and lymph drainage. Discharged with follow-up care, monitoring, and sun avoidance instructions.

A 57-year-old female with IgA nephropathy, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and end-stage renal disease was admitted post-kidney transplantation. She presented with visual disturbances and mild microalbuminuria, with a history of epilepsy, haemolysis, low platelets, proteinuria, and renal failure. A kidney biopsy revealed IgA nephropathy, necessitating peritoneal dialysis. A kidney transplant was performed at 52 years old, followed by severe heart failure and diastolic dysfunction. Post-transplant, a m.3243A>G mutation was identified, and immunosuppression therapy (prednisone and tacrolimus) was initiated. The patient is currently stable with kidney function and scheduled follow-up with a nephrologist.

The patient, [Name], was admitted on [Date] due to multiple cervicofacial lacerations caused by a broken beer bottle. He had a blood pressure of 70/40 mmHg, pulse of 110 bpm, and hemoglobin level of 4.7 mg/dl. CT angiography revealed contrast leakage in the right internal carotid artery, and stent insertion was performed at the laceration site. Surgery removed the hematoma and checked for injuries, with follow-up at the outpatient clinic. The patient was discharged on [Date] with antiplatelet medication and outpatient follow-up appointments.

The patient, a 29-year-old white male farmer, was admitted with left upper quadrant abdominal discomfort and unintentional weight loss. Initial examination revealed splenomegaly, elevated leukocyte count, low hemoglobin, and high platelet count. Laboratory results confirmed CML in chronic phase and hydroxyurea substitution with imatinib. Splenomegaly resolved within 3 months, but imatinib was discontinued due to pancytopenia. Bone marrow analysis showed complete remission of CML and Leishmania amastigotes. Treatment with pentavalent antimonials led to complete recovery, followed by initiation of TKI therapy. Acute cardiac toxicity required suspension, and amphotericin B was used. After 3 months, TKI therapy resumed, with a PCR showing deep molecular response. The patient was discharged with no further complications and recommended for follow-up care.

Discharge Summary:  
The 46-year-old male patient was admitted with B-symptoms, recurrent pneumonia, and lymphadenopathy. A computed tomography (CT) scan revealed enlarged liver and spleen and lymph nodes, including mediastinal and inguinal lymph nodes. He was diagnosed with CD hyaline vascular type and treated with six cycles of R-CHOP chemotherapy. After the fourth cycle, follow-up CT showed pulmonary artery dilation on the right with wall thickening and enlargement of hilar and subcarinal lymph nodes. Hemoptysis and erythema nodosum were diagnosed later, leading to Behcet’s Disease. Hydrocortisone, azathioprine, and enoxaparin were initiated. The patient is currently on prednisone, azathioprine, colchicine, and rivaroxaban, with follow-up appointments to assess rheumatology. Discharge diagnosis: Behcet’s Disease with pulmonary aneurysm.

The patient presented with burning, itching, pain, stinging, lacrimation, and decreased vision in her left eye, reporting sand splash at the seaside three months prior and discontinuation of contact lens use ten days before admission. A biomicroscopic examination revealed central keratitis and corneal scraping with Acanthamoeba sp. cysts identified in Giemsa-stained specimens. Treatment included alternating topical vancomycin, ceftazidime, propamidine isothionate, and chlorhexidine at the clinic. Contact lenses and solution were disposed of, resulting in no growth. Follow-up confirmed no infection after inoculation of the corneal scraping sample onto E. coli. The case was approved by the Ethics Committee at Uludag University (2016-9/18) and informed consent was obtained.

Discharge Summary:  
The patient, [redacted], was discharged with a pituitary germinoma diagnosis (central diabetes insipidus) following an eight-month course. Initial lab results confirmed hypopituitarism, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, polyuria, and hypertonic hypernatremia, along with a right-sided pituitary microadenoma. Hydrocortisone and levothyroxine were prescribed, and tumor markers and a water deprivation test confirmed central diabetes insipidus. Tumor markers were negative, and a transsphenoidal pituitary biopsy confirmed an intrasellar germinoma. The patient was stabilized with whole ventricle brain radiation and scheduled follow-ups with endocrinology to monitor treatment and symptoms.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient Information: [REDACTED], Male, 62 years, Medical Record Number [REDACTED], Admission Date [REDACTED], Discharge Date [REDACTED].  
Hospital Course: The patient was admitted due to early symptoms of memory decline and cognitive impairment. No prior history of brain injury or neuropsychological disease was noted. Symptoms worsened over 5 years, affecting daily functioning. Tests included MMSE, MoCA-B, CDR, and global deterioration scale, revealing severely impaired cognitive function. Cerebrospinal fluid tau, ptau, and Aβ1-42 levels were abnormal. A distinctively positive [C-11] Pittsburg compound B PET scan and [F-18] fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan with typical AD-like hypometabolic patterns were performed. Diagnosis: Cognitive impairment and AD-like hypometabolic pattern, indicating Alzheimer’s disease.  
Treatment: Not provided.  
Condition at Discharge: Stable.  
Plan of Care: Family advised follow-up with a primary care provider for continued monitoring. Care and support services were recommended to assist daily living.  
Follow-up: Follow-up with primary care provider for continued management.  
Signature: [REDACTED]  
Date and Time: [REDACTED]

A 19-year-old female patient with pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma was admitted for treatment of occupying lesions in the left adrenal and paraganglion regions, along with masses in the right lung and pancreas. She had a history of tumor removal from the right adrenal gland, with subsequent scans revealing multiple lesions. Symptomatic management included medications for fever, headache, and hypertension, and follow-up monitoring for further treatment. The final diagnosis was a combined presentation of pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma with lesions in specified areas. The patient is discharged with continued monitoring and follow-up.

A 17-year-old female patient underwent orthodontic treatment following 31 months of surgical orthodontic traction, resulting in an unfavorable outcome. Post-treatment, she opted for partial maxillary osteotomy (March 2, 2001), involving the removal of the right canine and a distal segment of the maxillary arch. Post-surgery, elastic traction was applied, and intermaxillary immobilization was sustained for 21 days, with continuous arch-wire replacement to stabilize the segment. Full orthodontic movements were cleared in April 2001, followed by the installation of removable retainers. A 10-year follow-up (January 10, 2012) confirmed excellent periodontal conditions, with the patient requesting removal of internal fixation on October 29, 2010.

The 87-year-old male was admitted with chest pain, light-headedness, and shortness of breath. On physical examination, he exhibited jugular venous distention and muffled heart sounds. He has a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, recent pulseless ventricular tachycardia, and nonischemic cardiomyopathy. No further treatment information was provided.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient: [REDACTED], Female, 54 years old, discharged on [REDACTED]. Admitted with a sodium hydroxide splash injury to the left eye, presenting symptoms of light perception issues and conjunctival congestion. Initial findings included a diffuse corneal epithelial defect, stromal edema, and Descemet’s folds. Treatment involved 1% dexamethasone, 1% atropine, and tobramycin. Prednisone (50 mg daily) was prescribed for 10 days, tapered gradually. Subconjunctival bevacizumab (0.05 ml, 1.25 mg) was administered to reduce corneal neovascularization, followed by topical use of 0.3% ofloxacin and 1% dexamethasone. Visual acuity improved to 0.1 LogMAR two weeks post-second injection, and neovascularization was reduced. The patient’s condition was well-controlled over 24 months, with no changes in visual acuity or clinical status.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient Information: [Redacted], Male, 51 years, admitted on [Redacted], discharged on N/A. Chief Complaint: Lymphadenopathy in the left neck, mediastinum, and right lung tubercle. Diagnosis: Stage IV pulmonary adenocarcinoma. Treatment: Four cycles of combination chemotherapy (nimotuzumab, pemetrexed, autologous lymphocyte reinfusion), three cycles of pembrolizumab, and whole brain radiation therapy. Procedures: Mediastinal lymphadenectomy, wedge resection of the right lower lobe, immunohistochemical analysis, and gene detection. Follow-up: 31 months post-pembrolizumab. Condition at Discharge: N/A. Discharge Medications: N/A.

The patient, [REDACTED], was admitted with heart failure and a renal artery aneurysm and arteriovenous fistula. They were effectively managed via endovascular occlusion, resolving symptoms and improving clinical status. Discharge instructions include follow-up with primary care, adherence to medications, a low-salt diet, and a healthy lifestyle.

Patient: Vietnamese, 55-year-old male, diagnosed with HBV cirrhosis without HDV, HCV, or HIV coinfections in 1997. Complications: Grade 1 oesophageal varices, Child Pugh A score. Treatment: Lamivudine (100 mg/day) initiated in 1998 due to undetectable HBV-DNA. Relapse in 1999, treatment continued with undetectable DNA and normal ALT. Breakthrough in 2002, resistant mutations detected. Treatment modified to adefovir and interferon, with ongoing resistance. Final treatment trial with tenofovir, leading to undetectable HBV-DNA. Patient now on liver transplantation.

The patient, a 2-day-old male newborn, was referred to us due to abnormal genitalia with a double penis and hypospadias, imperforate anus with distended bowel loops, and a duplicated recto-sigmoid colon. Laparotomy, colostomy, cystoplasty, and surgical exploration were performed, leading to the diagnosis of abnormal genitalia and genitourinary tract anomalies. The patient was discharged 2 weeks post-surgery with follow-up instructions for regular care and monitoring.

The 40-year-old female patient, diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and a history of ureteral stones, Behcet’s disease, and multiple myoma, underwent a laparoscopic-assisted myomectomy for infertility treatment. Timed intercourse was initiated, and standard treatment guidelines were followed, including cyclofenil (600 mg/d for 5 days) and chlormadinone acetate (4 mg/d for 10 days). A 48 × 41 mm anechoic mass in the right ovary was initially considered a follicle and monitored for follicular development, which was not observed by day 25. Subsequent mass sizes on days 16, 20, 21, and 28 indicated gradual mass changes, followed by disappearance on the 62nd day (19th day of the menstrual cycle). The mass was diagnosed as a high-occlusion (HOC) and discharged with follow-up monitoring.

The patient was diagnosed with paradoxical reaction, confirmed via CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy, and treated with updated anti-tuberculosis therapy. The new pulmonary mass was reduced, and symptoms improved. The patient is asymptomatic, with the original treatment continuing.

The patient, a 70-year-old female with no prior breast health issues, was admitted with skin changes in her left breast. A 3×3 cm pink lesion was found, and she agreed to an excisional biopsy. Diagnosis confirmed primary cutaneous ALCL, with no further treatment needed. She is recovering well and scheduled follow-up with oncology. Discharged on [Date].

Discharge Summary:  
Patient: [Patient's name], 70-year-old male with multiple comorbidities, presented with chest pain and palpitations. Initial evaluation diagnosed right ventricular outflow tract ventricular tachycardia (RVOT-VT) requiring external cardioversion. Subsequent management included intravenous amiodarone and left ventricular systolic dysfunction evaluation. The patient was diagnosed with obstructive coronary artery disease (OCA) years ago, unmanaged, and experienced recurrent RVOT-VT managed with amiodarone. Surgical options (resection, bypass, ICD) were explored, but he refused, leading to subcutaneous ICD placement. Discharged on prior medication regimen: aspirin, atorvastatin, digoxin, lisinopril, and spironolactone-hydrochlorothiazide. Follow-up appointments advised primary care and specialists, with discharge in stable condition. Medications continued as prescribed, and symptoms monitored.

A 22-year-old Indian female referred to Department of Periodontics for persistent lip swelling and recurrent angular cheilitis was diagnosed with oral Crohn’s disease without intestinal involvement. She received anti-inflammatory drugs, corticosteroid therapy, and topical steroids to manage oral ulcers and cheilitis. Subgingival scaling and external gingivectomy were planned. Follow-up showed no gastrointestinal symptoms, and blood tests remained stable. Although treatment improved symptoms, gingival recovery was not fully achieved.

Discharge Summary:  
The patient, [REDACTED], was discharged from the hospital with difficulty flushing the PEG tube and localized PEG-tube site pain. An external bulge was noted at the gastrostomy site, and the PEG tube experienced external migration, leading to BBS (bacterial blockage) suspicion. An EGD revealed a bulge at the fistula site, with an internal bumper embedded within the gastric lumen. External traction and PEG tube removal were performed without complications, followed by the placement of a 14 F, 1.7-cm Mic-Key® button over the guidewire. Kidney, ureter, and bladder X-rays showed no free air. The patient was discharged home without further hospital follow-up, with no prescribed medications. The diagnosis was difficulty flushing the PEG tube and localized pain.

A 6-year-old female patient with left-sided CMT and an incidental right-sided chest wall mass underwent a right posterolateral thoracotomy with tumor excision, release of the left SCM tendon, and partial removal of the fifth rib. Histopathology confirmed a desmoid tumor with negative margins, diagnosed based on imaging and pathology findings. The patient is to be closely monitored for recurrence and follow-up with oncology.

Patient Name: [MP]

Admitting Diagnosis: Chronic pain syndrome with failed back surgery syndrome (FBSS)  

The patient, with a long-standing history of intractable chronic pain in both lower back and legs, received combined spinal cord stimulation (SCS) and deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the periaqueductal gray (PVG) for treatment. Post-surgery, mixed pain components (neuropathic radicular and nociceptive) were resolved, with SCS providing complete relief for leg pain but not the axial lower back. DBS achieved excellent axial pain relief, and follow-up maintenance of the neuromodulation systems resulted in pain-free outcomes. The patient has been free of chronic pain for 22 years and resumed normal activities. Follow-up care includes regular reprogramming visits.  

Signed, [Insert Name of Physician]

A 76-year-old male presents with exertional dyspnea, visual disturbances, night sweats, and progressive fatigue. His history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, and alcohol abuse. Physical examination reveals petechiae and hematoma in lower extremities, with elevated white blood cell count, low hemoglobin, and platelet count. The peripheral blood smear shows a large number of blasts and promyelocytes, resembling APL, along with elevated LDH and creatinine levels. Treatment involves leukapheresis, chemotherapy, and ATRA. The patient's condition improved, and he was discharged with appropriate care instructions.

A 67-year-old Hispanic male was admitted with generalized body weakness, difficulty sleeping, abdominal pain, increased thirst with urinary frequency, and constipation. Diagnosed with poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with squamous features suggestive of pancreaticobiliary primary. Chemotherapy with cisplatin and gemcitabine was initiated, but the patient had recurrent admissions with worsening symptoms and uncontrolled hypercalcemia. His course was complicated further by acute kidney injury, cholestatic hyperbilirubinemia, pancreatitis, and percutaneous transhepatic cholecystostomy (PTC). The patient ultimately expired within three months of his diagnosis.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient: Case 8, 30-year-old female  
Chief Complaint: Elevated CK, episodes of palpitation  
Hospital Course: Admitted for further evaluation of elevated CK and palpitations. Initial ECG showed T wave inversion, TTE normal. Genetic testing revealed a heterozygous carrier of a missense variant in COL6A1 gene (c.1273-4T>C), VUS. Patient monitored overnight and followed outpatient follow-up with ECG, Holter, and exercise stress testing. Consultation recommended medication for systemic lupus, primary care for CK, and cardiology for palpitations. Genetic counseling and orthopedic follow-up for myalgia were advised. Discharged with instructions to follow up.

Brief Hospital Course:  
A 29-year-old female medical microbiologist in training was admitted on [Redacted] with symptoms of low-grade fever, general malaise, and retro-orbital headache following mosquito exposure in Suriname. She developed a maculopapular rash on trunk and extremities, conjunctival injection, and stiffness/edema in wrists, knees, and ankles. Contact lens intolerance was noted, but symptoms resolved after 7 days.  

Diagnostic Assessment:  
Diagnosis confirmed ZIKV infection via urine and plasma testing (qRT-PCR, manuscript in progress).  

Summary of Events:  
Diagnosed with ZIKV infection after returning from Suriname. Presented with fever, rash, swelling, and contact lens intolerance. Discharged after 7 days of observation.  

Follow-Up:  
Follow-up instructions deferred further management. Discharged home in stable condition.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient Name: [Patient Name]  
MR#: [Medical Record Number]  

The patient, a 62-year-old male with a history of tobacco abuse and newly diagnosed small-cell lung cancer, was readmitted to the hospital with shortness of breath. Over the previous month, he had been on chemotherapy and radiation. Four days prior, he was diagnosed with acute idiopathic pericarditis, starting medication. Upon admission, he exhibited signs of pericardial effusion (marked jugular venous distension, Kussmaul's sign absent, and ST-segment elevation), with significant lab findings (low WBC/leukocyte, elevated creatinine, urea, and lactate). An electrocardiogram showed normal voltage, and urgent echocardiography revealed tamponade and right ventricular failure. Emergency pericardiocentesis drained 800 mL of green fluid. Antibiotics were tailored for purulent pericarditis. Partial pericardiectomy and sepsis resolved. The source of the polymicrobial pericarditis was unclear, but the patient was discharged home on day 8. No recurrence of effusion was noted 4 weeks post-discharge, and he resumed chemo-radiation therapy 2 months later.

**Hospital Course:**  
15-year-old female admitted for suicidal ideation and self-harm due to trauma-related stress. Reported anxiety and intrusive thoughts following a high school traumatic event. Daily therapy and family sessions were conducted.  

**Discharge Diagnosis:**  
PTSD with symptoms of intrusive thoughts, recurrent nightmares, panic attacks, and suicidal ideation.  

**Discharge Medications:** None. Parents declined pharmacologic treatment.  

**Follow-Up Plan:**  
Home follow-up in Youth Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) three days a week. Therapy addresses coping and non-pharmacological strategies.  

**Discharge Condition:**  
Stable, discharged with IOP instructions. Parents educated on follow-up and support.  

**Discharge Instructions:**  
Attend therapy sessions as scheduled, practice coping skills, and seek immediate help for suicidal ideation or self-harm.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]  
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]  
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]  

Chief Complaint: The patient was admitted with a diagnosis of invasive low-grade carcinoma of the appendix colonizing appendicial endometriosis.  

History: A 45-year-old female was admitted to the hospital for a second look laparotomy and HIPEC following a previous diagnosis of acute appendicitis, along with multiple peritoneal mucinous implants in the right pelvis.  

Hospital Course: The patient underwent right hemicolectomy, resection of two segments of small intestine, omentectomy, bilateral ovariectomy, and peritoneal resections with HIPEC administration. Pathology revealed foci of endometriosis on the ileal surface of the right hemicolectomy specimen, the left Fallopian tube, and in one of the peritoneal fragments. Free intrabdominal mucin was absent, and acellular mucin was localized on the right peritoneal surface. Both ovaries had functional cysts. The patient’s clinical course was uneventful for 18 months.  

Diagnosis: Invasive low-grade carcinoma of the appendix colonizing appendicial endometriosis.  

Treatment: Right hemicolectomy, resection of two segments of small intestine, omentectomy, bilateral ovariectomy, and peritoneal resections with HIPEC administration.  

Condition on Discharge: Stable.  

Follow-up: Close outpatient follow-up is recommended.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient Name: [redacted]  
Age: 9  
Gender: Male  

**History of Present Illness:** The patient presented with recurrent abdominal pain in the left lumbar region for 4 years. A renal ultrasound revealed left hydronephrosis, and a cystoscopy identified a 4–5 cm ureteral narrowing. Cohen’s ureteroneocystostomy was performed, which resolved the issue. The patient recovered uneventfully and completed a one-year follow-up with no further treatment needed.  

**Diagnosis:** Incomplete duplication of the right side with left hydronephrosis and hydroureter.  

**Procedures:** Cohen’s ureteroneocystostomy.  

**Discharge:** Stable.  

**Follow-up:** Regular follow-ups advised. No further treatment required.

The patient was diagnosed with B-cell ALL and underwent induction chemotherapy, double-delayed intensification, and maintenance therapy. A CNS relapse was treated with the same CCG-1882 protocol along with whole brain and spine irradiation during consolidation. Four months after the initial relapse, a second relapse occurred with ≥90% leukemic blasts in the bone marrow, which was treated with aggressive reinduction chemotherapy. The patient died 3 months after the second relapse.

The patient, male, 74 years old, presented with repeated cough, expectoration, and wheezing for 8 years, along with chest pain and shortness of breath for 7 days. Initial diagnosis was chronic bronchitis and bronchial anthracofibrosis in the right middle lobe, but after exacerbation and further testing, it was revised to tuberculous pleuritis. Post-treatment, symptoms resolved, and the patient was discharged in stable condition with outpatient follow-up.

The patient, a female with a history of SLE, DM, hypertension, and cataracts, was admitted with multifocal pneumonia and multiple infections, including Pneumocystis jiroveci and other pathogens. She received IV antibiotics and underwent intubation and tracheostomy. Despite persistent fevers, treatment for P. wickerhamii resolved the infection, and follow-up care will continue with primary care. Medications will be adjusted as prescribed.

A 67-year-old man with intermittent headache and hypomnesia was admitted to the hospital and discharged after five months of treatment, with a high-dose methotrexate and idarubicin regimen. His serum lactate dehydrogenase level and cerebrospinal fluid protein were elevated, leading to partial remission. The International Extranodal Lymphoma Study Group score classified him as a high-risk group, and no follow-up plan was necessary due to his death.

The patient, a 36-year-old male with Wilson's disease, was admitted for operative, periodontal, and prosthodontic treatments due to severe dental caries and generalized gingivitis. Procedures were performed under general anesthesia in two minimal visits, with continuous monitoring of vital signs, IV lines, and end-tidal gases. The patient was intubated and monitored for response entropy and state entropy. An incidentally found gold crown slid during a try-in, which was promptly removed, and gauze packing was used to prevent recurrence. Discharge was successful with no complications, and follow-up instructions included routine medication, oral hygiene, and medical follow-up.

A 60-year-old female presented with shortness of breath, palpitations, chest pain, and progressive dyspnea. She had a history of dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea. Physical examination revealed arterial blood pressure of 135/90 mmHg, heart rate of 110 bpm, SpO₂ 94%, and respiratory rate of 24 breaths/min. No significant medical history was noted. Diagnostic testing showed normal cardiac enzymes and complete blood count, with eosinophilia. Chest radiography showed cardiomegaly and left heart board, and ECG indicated normal sinus rhythm with no ST segment changes. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large multicystic mass from the left ventricle to the pericardium, confirmed by CT. A serologic test for hydatidosis was positive, and a well-defined, thin-walled, homogeneous multiple cardiac hydatid cyst was confirmed. Post-surgery, pain was managed with bupivacain, tramadol, and diclofenac, and the patient was discharged with no complications. Follow-up was uneventful, and the patient was advised for further management.

Patient: [Redacted]  
Date: [Redacted]

Hospital Course: A 68-year-old Japanese man underwent resection for leiomyosarcoma at the mediastinum, followed by radiation therapy and a second operation. Post-surgery, CT scans showed improved outcomes with a non-enhanced cystic lesion and a smaller solid lesion in the left lung. RFA (radiofrequency ablation) was performed after chemotherapy, with three sessions (20–80 W) and a total ablation time of 57 minutes. Pain and tumor growth reappeared three months post-RFA, leading to discharge with follow-up instructions.

A 17-year-old Saudi male with bronchial asthma was admitted to the emergency department with dyspnea, nonproductive cough, and wheezing for 48 hours. He had a history of two hospitalizations for worsening symptoms. On examination, vital signs were normal except for dyspnea, with SPO2 89% and RR 28/min. CT revealed subcutaneous, mediastinal, and posterior spinal emphysema, along with air in the pericardium and epidural spaces. Treatment included broad-spectrum antibiotics, bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and oxygen. The patient was discharged with a follow-up to monitor symptoms and consult with primary care and pulmonologists.

Clinical Course:  
The patient was admitted to the KLE Ayurveda Hospital for treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. She was prescribed Agnitundi vati, Valuka Sweda, and Dashanga Lepa. Symptoms of itching, redness, and rashes occurred around the area of application of Dashanga Lepa, which were resolved with local application of Shatadoutha Ghritha. A month later, she was treated again with Shatadoutha Ghritha, leading to complete relief of symptoms within three days.  

Hospital Course:  
- Admitted for rheumatoid arthritis treatment.  
- Developed symptoms after Dashanga Lepa application.  
- Treated with Shatadoutha Ghritha.  
- Improved symptoms within two days.  
- Admitted for second treatment.  

Patient Information:  
- Patient: 42-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis.  
- Diabetes history: Metformin management.  
- Prakruti: Pitta kapha.  

Discharge Plan:  
- Discharged without Dashanga Lepa.  
- Advised to update physician for allergic reactions.  
- Educated on medication and allergy records.  
- Follow-up with treating physician if symptoms recur.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient: [REDACTED]  
Medical Record: [REDACTED]  

Final Diagnosis:  
- Streptococcus salivarius meningitis  
- Antiphospholipid syndrome  
- Cerebrospinal fluid leak (CSF-L)  
- Ventriculitis  
- Encephalopathy  

Hospital Course:  
Admitted with acute worsening of headache, new-onset neck/back pain, photophobia, chills, and pain. Laboratory findings: cloudy CSF, glucose <10 mg/dL, protein 732 mg/dL, nucleated cells 2764/uL, segmented neutrophils. CSF Gram-positive cocci, Streptococcus salivarius growth. IV dexamethasone, cefepime, vancomycin, lumbar puncture. Bilateral endoscopic ethmoid repair with lumbar drain, ventriculostomy placement. Complicated post-repair CSF leak and ventriculitis. CSF studies resolved, ventriculo-peritoneal shunt placed.  

Follow-up:  
- Monitor antiphospholipid syndrome and CSF-L  
- Continue apixaban  
- Follow specialists (OTOL/NEUROSURG)  
- Complete antibiotic course  

Plan:  
Follow up with primary care, continue apixaban, and adhere to prescribed antibiotic regimen. Educated on medication compliance and follow-up care.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient 2, 23 months old, presented with fever and diagnostic criteria for sJIA (complicated by MAS) on admission and discharged on oral steroids. She was treated with IVIG and high-dose ASA, but developed polyarthritis, serositis, and MAS. After high-dose IVMP, she defervished and improved clinically. Follow-up echocardiograms showed coronary artery dilatation resolved six weeks post-diagnosis. Discharge recommendations include continued low-dose prednisone as maintenance therapy and follow-up appointments with rheumatology and cardiology.

The patient was admitted for evaluation of fatigue and weakness with a suspected recurrence of metastatic germ cell tumor. A bone marrow biopsy revealed acute megakaryoblastic leukemia, diagnosed based on pancytopenia, blasts, and negative staining for myeloperoxidase and leukocyte common antigen. Treatment with daunorubicin and cytarabin was initiated six months post-diagnosis, followed by a cervical lymph node FNA showing blast-rich marrow. Discharge summary notes follow-up appointments for monitoring.

The patient, a 25-year-old gravida 3, para 2002 at 32 0/7 weeks' gestation, was admitted with intermittent severe abdominal pain and obstipation. She had a history of hypothyroidism, microcytic anemia, and sigmoid volvulus in her previous pregnancy. On physical examination, suprapubic and right lower quadrant tenderness were noted, with normal bowel sounds. A confirmed singleton fetus was detected on obstetric ultrasound. Abdominal radiography showed colonic distention, and laboratory evaluation was unremarkable. Colonoscopic decompression was performed with a rectal tube, leading to a successful procedure. However, symptoms recurred at 37 0/7 weeks. A second decompression was done, resulting in labor and a vaginal delivery of a healthy infant. Postpartum complications included worsening abdominal pain confirmed by CT, recurrence of volvulus, and a fourth decompression. The patient was discharged with a benign histopathology and follow-up care scheduled.

The 46-year-old male patient, admitted with maxillary anterior pain and swelling, underwent endodontic treatment. Subsequent swelling worsened, with a diagnosis of an infected dentigerous cyst confirmed post-surgery. The lesion was surgically removed along with the impacted mesiodens, and follow-up care is recommended.

Discharge Summary:  
A 62-year-old man with rectal carcinoma was admitted for neoadjuvant chemotherapy. On day 4, he experienced sudden inability to speak, leading to an MRI showing significant diffusion restriction in frontal white matter and splenium. 5-FU was discontinued, and he recovered fully. MRI results showed resolution, and he was discharged after being cleared. The diagnosis was a transient ischemic attack (TIA), with 5-FU contributing. No further treatment was required, and follow-up care includes post-discharge visits.

A 70-year-old male with a right femoral neck fracture due to age-related osteoporosis presented post-fall at home. After undergoing posterior hemi arthroplasty with a cemented bipolar prosthesis, the patient experienced right hip clicking on day 5 post-op. Radiographs showed prosthesis dissociation at the femoral head-neck junction, with the femoral head intact and the stem/neck components intact. Open reduction and reassembly were performed, and follow-up after 1 year confirmed a favorable outcome, with no complications. The patient is currently asymptomatic and has a new femoral head with proper alignment.

The patient, a 61-year-old male, was admitted to our hospital in October 2017 for an irritable cough. He was diagnosed with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with EGFR exon 19 deletion and MET amplification. Initial treatment included gefitinib therapy, followed by combination therapy with gefitinib and crizotinib. Salvage therapy involved immunotherapy and chemotherapy, resulting in significant improvement. The patient’s condition was monitored with regular follow-ups, and he maintained improved quality of life with no pulmonary symptoms. Discharge diagnosis: stage IV NSCLC.

Discharge Date: [date]

Principal Diagnosis: Mesenteric ischemia secondary to atypical fibromuscular dysplasia.  

Hospital Course:  
The patient was admitted with complaints of intractable abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea. She had a history of hypertension and preeclampsia, and took oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) for 15 years. Tests (colonoscopy, MRA) revealed nonspecific findings and a 6 × 15 Palmaz Blue Angioplasty stent was placed. Symptom improvement was noted, with follow-up instructions for dietary and medical follow-up.

5. Contact physician immediately for symptoms like abdominal pain.

Discharge Summary:  
An 18-year-old male undergraduate student with growth retardation, abdominal swelling, and disproportionate limb enlargement was diagnosed with Klippel-Tre'naunay syndrome based on clinical presentations. He had kyphoscoliosis, left gynecomastia, and right lower limb overgrowth, including toes, with splenomegaly. Physical findings included nevi over the right flank and leg, secondary edema, and eczematous skin changes. Lab results showed trilineage suppression and normal bone marrow, with venous malformations absent. Comorbidities were not reported, and follow-up evaluations are recommended. Discharge condition stable with no further interventions.

The patient, [Name], presented with a recurrent schwannoma arising from the middle cranial base and sunken eye and upper eyelid drooping. A three-stage surgical plan was executed, including autologous grafts (costal cartilage, auricular cartilage, and fascia lata) for eye socket, lower eyelid, and upper eyelid correction. Post-op follow-ups showed improvement in appearance but partial correction of enophthalmos. Discharged without complications, with scheduled follow-ups as instructed. Final diagnosis: recurrent schwannoma. Discharge medications: N/A.

Discharge Summary  
Patient Name: [REDACTED]  
DOB: [REDACTED]  
Gender: Male  

Clinical History: A 22-year-old male with non-seminomatous germinal tumor (NSGT-E-IB) underwent left inguinal orchiectomy, revealing mixed germ cells including embryonal carcinoma, mature teratoma, and seminoma. Two BEP cycles (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin) were administered, followed by yearly follow-up. Eleven years later, the patient underwent a neurological consultation for MS-related visual acuity loss, which was confirmed with interferon β-1a treatment. Subsequent follow-up revealed improved clinical outcomes, including a decrease in AFP levels and PET scans showing increased uptake in the left supraclavicular region and lungs.  

Medical Course: Initial BEP therapy led to disease progression, followed by BOMP-EPI cycles. A complete response was achieved after two cycles, with continued treatment. Subsequent therapy included taxol, ifosfamide, and carboplatin, alongside cisplatin substitution. Radiotherapy was administered, but the patient declined further treatment. The patient’s condition worsened, and a coma was observed after a large cerebral hemorrhage, leading to his death.  

Assessment and Plan: The patient had significant past medical history (NSGT-E1B, MS) and a progressive worsening course. Despite aggressive management, the patient died post-hospitalization. Follow-up has been initiated at the discretion of the patient’s family.

91-year-old Japanese woman with history of acute-onset type 1 diabetes and absolute insulin deficiency, on premixed biphasic insulin aspart, miglitol, aliskiren, sitagliptin (25 mg/day), and HbA1c 9.6% prior to 24-week treatment. Post-meal glucose 252 mg/dl, HbA1c reduced from 9.6% to 7.4% over 24 weeks, with aliskiren replaced by candesartan. C-peptide remains undetectable (below 0.1 ng/ml), no adverse events observed in kidneys/liver, gastrointestinal, or weight gain. No diet/exercise changes noted in follow-up.

The patient, a 40-year-old female admitted with suspected organophosphorus poisoning, was treated with atropine and parenteral hydration, leading to gradual improvement. After a 12-hour course, she regained consciousness, and on day 7, she developed delayed onset intermediate syndrome requiring ICU treatment. Treatment intensified with pralidoxime, and she was discharged on day 22. Follow-up confirmed full recovery, with the patient able to resume routine work.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient Information:  
- Name: [Patient’s name]  
- Age: 38  
- Gender: Female  

Diagnosis:  
- Recurrent ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast  

Hospital Course:  
- Patient underwent total mastectomy with immediate reconstruction due to recurrence.  
- Previous whole-breast irradiation was administered.  
- Patient opted for DIEP flap reconstruction as a suitable choice for active running.  

Procedure:  
- A stacked DIEP flap using both hemi-abdominal flaps was performed.  
- Two single perforators were selected and dissected to their respective deep inferior epigastric pedicles.  
- One set of vessels was anastomosed to the antegrade internal mammary vessels, while the other set was anastomosed to the retrograde internal mammary vessels.  

Outcomes:  
- Satisfactory aesthetic outcome with good size match achieved without fat necrosis.  
- Computed tomography angiogram (CTA) of the chest was performed incidentally for respiratory concerns, revealing patent vascular anastomoses to both pedicles.  

Follow-up:  
- Patient was discharged with wound care and scheduled follow-up appointments.  
- One-year follow-up confirmed a satisfactory aesthetic outcome with no complications.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient: [N/A], Female, 35 years. Admitted with a breast nodule in the upper right region. History of stage IV B-cell lymphoma treated with high-dose sequential (HDS) chemotherapy and autologous stem-cell transplantation with complete remission. Diagnosis of myeloid sarcoma based on morphologic and phenotypic findings. Initial imaging showed a recurrent disease, with a solitary mass diagnosed as myeloid sarcoma. Subsequent tests confirmed normal blood counts, no blasts, and no leukemic infiltration. Treatment included radiotherapy and two courses of high-dose cytarabine, but relapsed after 5 months, leading to the patient's death in a fulminant course.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient Name: [Name]  
Medical Record Number: [Number]  
Admission Date: [Date]  
Discharge Date: [Date]  

Hospital Course:  
The patient was admitted to the national hospital of Sri Lanka on September [Date] with symptoms of dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and headache. Upon admission, the patient exhibited orange-red discoloration of the face, hands, and feet, and was drowsy but oriented and rational. No evidence of asterixis or coagulopathy was found. The patient had a history of deliberate self-harm, ingesting 28 tablets of FDC-IR (4.2 g INH and 7.2 g rifampicin), prescribed for her uncle. Family attempts at induced emesis were unsuccessful. The patient developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures (3 minutes) while being treated in the medical ward, leading to IV diazepam 5 mg administration. She was transferred to the hospital immediately for further care. Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.36, HCO3- 20 mmol/L, PCO2 24 mmHg, pO2 135 mmHg, Base excess -5, lactate 2.3, and O2 saturation 100%.  

Care Summary:  
Initial treatment included crushed oral pyridoxine 4.2 g and IV 0.9% saline to enhance excretion of toxic metabolites via kidneys. Supportive care for acute liver injury began on Day 2, with liver functions improving by Day 7. The patient made a complete recovery and was discharged on Day 10 of hospital admission. Post-discharge liver function tests were normal.

The patient, [NAME], presented with sudden onset of thunderclap headaches for three days, diagnosed with acute reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) following CTA and MRA findings. After testing, RCVS was suspected due to the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (IUS) and treatment included nimodipine and removal of the IUS. The patient’s symptoms improved, with stenosis resolving in one year. Discharge was made with resolved symptoms. Follow-up care is advised.

The patient was diagnosed with Pleomorphic Angiosarcoma of the pulmonary artery, confirmed as a myxoma (Pleomorphic Angiosarcoma, PAIS), following a high-throughput molecular screening and pulmonary biopsy. They initiated 4th-line chemotherapy (carboplatin + vinorelbinine) in February 2017, with a PS of 0 at 9 cycles, followed by progressive disease confirmed by CT scans. Next steps include stereotactic radiotherapy for the two progressing lesions.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient Name: N/A  
Age: 9 months  
Sex: Male  

Clinical Course: The patient presented with 8-day history of watery, non-bloody diarrhea, vomiting, and decreased oral intake. Initial investigations showed leukocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolysis, and microangiopathic hemolysis. Abdominal ultrasound revealed echogenic but normal-sized kidneys, confirming hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) caused by Norovirus GI/GII. Peritoneal dialysis was initiated after a lack of response to high doses of furosemide. Stool studies showed positive Norovirus GI/GII, with massive albuminuria and low complement levels.  

Treatment: Peritoneal dialysis for 5 days and one unit of packed red blood cells transfused.  

Outcome: Improved steadily, with normalization of kidney function and albuminuria, and C3/C4 complement levels returning to normal. Follow-up was completed with parents advised to continue routine pediatrician visits and a healthy lifestyle. No follow-up testing was mentioned in the case report.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient Name: [insert patient name]  
Gender: Male  
Age: 41 years old  
Date of Admission: [insert date]  
Date of Discharge: [insert date]  

Reason for Admission: Admitted for closure of an open, infected wound on the right lower limb following an accidental explosion.  

Hospital Course:  
- Initial vital signs: BP 99/50 mmHg, HR 102 bpm, RR 21 breaths/min.  
- Medical history: No chronic conditions, no unhealthy behaviors.  
- Aggressive treatment: Fluid administration, hemodynamic support, antibiotic therapy.  
- Two surgeries: Debridement, necrotic muscle excision, wound closure with VSD and drainage.  
- Stretching therapy applied. Wound size decreased from 40×35 cm to 1.0×0.8 cm in 18 days.  

Discharge Condition: Wounds healed, skin margins intact, patient ambulated and performed activities.  

Instructions for Outpatient Care:  
- Maintain wound site cleanliness and dressings.  
- Avoid overexertion.  
- Seek medical attention for complications.  

Follow-Up:  
- Continue outpatient care, monitor wound healing, and follow physician guidelines.

The 85-year-old Japanese woman with squamous cell lung carcinoma was admitted with rapidly worsening general fatigue and appetite loss eight days after the eighth cycle of pembrolizumab monotherapy. She had been diagnosed with Stage IV squamous cell lung cancer seven months prior, with stable disease following pembrolizumab. Routine examinations before each infusion showed no significant changes up to the eighth cycle. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities, while laboratory results showed isolated ACTH deficiency, with hydrocortisone improving general condition, normalizing cortisol levels, and correcting ADH and sodium imbalances. Follow-up showed no further changes in ACTH or cortisol levels, with normal thyroid function and other parameters.

Hospital Course Summary:  
Admission: A 35-year-old female admitted with worsening headaches, initially diagnosed with migraine. Prescribed propranolol and flunarazine, followed by discharge.  
Readmission: Readmitted one month later with persistent headaches and bilateral -0.5 diopter refractive error. Topiramate prescribed for two weeks, followed by discontinuation and referral to ophthalmologist.  

Discharge: Diagnosed with topiramate-induced acute myopia, resolved with no complications.  

Follow-up: Advised to avoid topiramate, scheduled follow-ups with general practitioner and ophthalmologist.  

Diagnostic Test Results:  
- Neurological examination: Normal  
- Ophthalmological examination: Bilateral -0.5 diopters refractive error  
- Vision: 6/6  
- Intraocular pressure: Normal  

Diagnosis: Topiramate-induced acute myopia  
Treatment: Discontinued topiramate.

Patient Name: [redacted]  
Medical Record Number: [redacted]  
Date of Admission: [redacted]  
Date of Discharge: [redacted]  

Admission Diagnosis: Epigastric pain, vomiting  
Discharge Diagnosis: Symptomatic cystic lymphangioma originating from the left adrenal gland  

Hospital Course:  
The patient was admitted with epigastric pain and vomiting, accompanied by multiple episodes. CT scans and MRIs confirmed a retroperitoneal cystic mass, which was surgically resected. Histopathology confirmed a cystic lymphangioma.  

Follow-up:  
The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5, with no recurrence of symptoms. Histopathology confirmed cystic lymphangioma.  

Differential Diagnosis:  
Primary adrenal tumors, metastatic adenocarcinomas, angiosarcomas, multicystic mesotheliomas, or adrenal cysts.  

Treatment:  
Surgical resection is recommended for symptomatic cystic lymphangioma. Adrenalectomy is performed if cyst origin is confirmed.  

Discharge Condition:  
Patient was discharged in stable condition. Follow-up is scheduled for outpatient clinic.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient Name: [Redacted]  
Date of Admission: [Redacted]  
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]  
Length of Stay: [Redacted]  

Diagnosis:  
Gross Hydronephrosis (GH) caused by obstruction from a kidney stone at the junction of the ureter and renal pelvis, accompanied by renal cell transitional cell carcinoma (T2N0M0).  

Hospital Course:  
The patient presented with abdominal girth increase, abdominal distension, and intermittent nausea over 2 years. Repeated intractable hiccups for 2 months led to hospital admission. Physical findings included a longitudinal surgical scar on the upper abdomen and a mass on the left side.  

Further investigations: ultrasonography, CT, and isotope kidney scan revealed a massive hypoechoic lesion occupying the abdomen, causing pressure on the stomach, liver, pancreas, and spleen. Adhesion was noted during laparoscopy and open nephrectomy.  

7.5 liters of hydronephrosis fluid was drained, and the left kidney and upper ureter removed, resolving hiccups and improving appetite. Post-op follow-up: no recurrence of hiccups.  

Discharge Instructions:  
Follow a proper diet and continue regular follow-up appointments with the healthcare provider.  

Signed electronically by: [Redacted]

The patient, a 18-month-old female, was admitted with mild fever and intermittent sinus discharge in the mid-dorsal area. She underwent a dorsal D1-D8 laminectomy, mid-line myelotomy, and total tumor excision under microscope, with intra-operative and post-operative methylprednisolone injections. Post-operatively, she developed mild weakness in the left lower limb, which was resolved by the 10th post-operative day. The histopathological diagnosis confirmed a dermoid cyst.

Patient: [Redacted]  
Admission: September 2004  
Discharge: N/A  

Hospital Course: A 41-year-old male presented with acute gastrointestinal bleeding and non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. Transferred to a larger center for R-CHOP chemotherapy, which failed. Subsequently, a surgical procedure was performed, with findings consistent with an infiltrative carcinoma, neuroendocrine tumor, and lymphoma. Octreotide was used until clinical recovery, and treatment was withheld.  

Diagnosis: Low-grade neuroendocrine tumor, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), and marginal zone B-cell lymphoma/chronic lymphocytic leukemia.  

Treatment: Octreotide acetate for clinical response; 3 R-CHOP cycles, 6 CHOP cycles, and subsequent treatment. CLL is under surveillance.  

Discharge: Monitor CLL and follow up for future concerns.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient [REDACTED] was discharged after a 10-year hospital course with the following findings:  
- Known 22q11DS (cardiac anomalies), conductive hearing loss bilaterally, malformed ossicular chain, narrow ear canals, and epitympanic ossicular fixation on the left side.  
- Tympanostomy tube placed at age 3, hearing aids worn since age 4, and middle ear inspection/ossicular reconstruction (left side) due to conductive hearing loss and narrow ear canals.  
- CT scan pre-op showed epitympanic ossicular fixation and horizontal orientation of the incus and dehiscent facial nerve canal on the left.  
- Retroauricular incision, external auditory canal widening, and malleus reconstruction resulted in a mobile ossicular chain.  
- Audiometry improved frequencies 0.25–2 kHz.  
Follow-up: Regular audiology testing.  

Diagnoses: 22q11DS, cardiac anomalies, conductive hearing loss, malformed ossicular chain, narrow ear canals, epitympanic fixation, horizontal incus orientation, and facial nerve canal.  
Procedures: Tympanostomy tube placement, middle ear inspection/ossicular reconstruction.

A 65-year-old male with diabetes, hypertension, and a spinal cord injury presented with high fever postoperative day 10 following partial lung resection for adenocarcinoma. CT scan revealed empyema, confirmed by Streptococcus caprae wound culture, and was treated with irrigation, drainage, and broad-spectrum antibiotics for 16 days. Despite reduction in infection size, it persisted. On day 36, non-open wound therapy with Negative Pressure Wound Therapy (NPWTi-d) was initiated, leading to continuous treatment for 20 days. Follow-up showed no recurrence of empyema, and the patient was discharged with regular follow-up to his primary care physician. The multidisciplinary team's efforts led to successful treatment and no further complications.

A five-year-old female cousin of Case-2 presents with a unique skeletal phenotype characterized by abnormal craniofacial contour, severe osteolysis in the shoulders and hips, and deformed pelvis. Radiographic studies revealed brachycephaly, scaphocephaly, total sagittal suture synostosis, and mild plagiocephaly in Case-2, while Case-1 shows brachycephaly and partial coronal/lambdoid closure, and Case-4 has clavicular hypoplasia. Case-5 exhibits a shepherd's crook deformity with coxa vara. Further diagnostic and therapeutic interventions may be required.

Discharge Summary:  
An 81-year-old Japanese male patient with squamous cell carcinoma was admitted June 25, 2009, for a mass in the right lingual margin. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed a soft tissue mass, leading to tumor resection under general anesthesia. Follow-up CT scans over six years showed no recurrence or metastasis, with a pathologic fracture detected in the clavicle. The patient's condition remains stable, and regular follow-up CT scans are recommended to monitor for cancer recurrence or metastasis.

Discharge summary:  
Patient [Redacted], male, 55 years old, admitted and discharged. Admitted with hypertension, high cholesterol, coronary artery disease, and two episodes of cough with hemoptysis. Discharged with a history of surgical intervention and pseudoaneurysm of SVG graft. The procedure involved percutaneous repair and intracoronary stenting, with no complications. Follow-up scheduled for six months. Discharge instructions include dual antiplatelet therapy and follow-up.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient Name: [redacted], Male, 3 years old, discharged on [redacted]. No post-operative complications reported. The patient was advised to attend follow-up sessions for further evaluations. The cause of left knee pain and epiphyseal overgrowth remains unclear, requiring further investigation.

The patient, [REDACTED], was discharged after a complex surgical procedure for a transverse colon lipomatous lesion resection. Abdominal imaging revealed a pseudo kidney, colocolic intussusception, and a 9 cm thickened colon segment. Histopathology confirmed a benign lipomatous lesion, and the post-op course was uneventful. The patient was discharged with instructions for wound care and symptom management, and a follow-up appointment scheduled with the surgeon within four weeks.

A 23-year-old male admitted with biliary cirrhosis and recent abdominal pain/jaundice underwent a successful emergency liver transplant. Post-transplant complications included severe polyneuropathy and multi-organ failure, which resolved on post-operative day 104, though further treatment and monitoring were needed.

Anonymous, a 72-year-old man with no diagnosed conditions, was admitted for subdural empyema and chronic subdural hematoma. After conservative management, a craniotomy was performed, with a thickened capsule and pus drainage. Histopathology confirmed the diagnosis, and follow-up care included oral minocycline therapy. Discharge was made without complications, and follow-up with the physician is recommended.

The patient was a preterm baby delivered vaginally at 34 weeks gestation with gross anomalies including a narrow chest, fused lower limbs and feet, absence of external genitalia, imperforate anus, and single umbilical artery. Investigation revealed diabetes mellitus in the mother. Despite aggressive medical management, the patient died due to severe respiratory distress. On autopsy, bilateral renal agenesis, two pea-sized gonads (testes), and disruptions in the gastrointestinal tract were observed.

The patient, a 35-year-old male with a history of arterial hypertension, left total hip replacement, avascular necrosis, and chronic convulsive syndrome, was admitted for progressive memory impairment, left hemiparesis, and language disorder. A brain biopsy revealed necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis. Autoimmune, infectious, and malignant diseases were ruled out, and treatment with cyclophosphamide and methylprednisolone was initiated. Two years later, the patient returned with aggressive behavior, mutism, incontinence, and worsening neurological symptoms, which were confirmed by a new brain MRI showing two frontoparietal and left cerebellar inflammatory lesions. Despite treatment, the condition continued to deteriorate and the patient ultimately died. The diagnosis was necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis, and the summary concludes his history with the progression of the disease and the outcome of death.

A 68-year-old female with a history of metastatic melanoma, hypertension, deep vein thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism was discharged with immunotherapy-induced RTA (final diagnosis) following admission for altered mental status, hypotension, and fever. She received a second dose of ipilimumab and nivolumab, managed for sepsis and multiorgan failure. Initial lab results showed hypotension, elevated WBC, and metabolic parameters, with a PT/INR and aPTT within normal ranges. The patient was transitioned to prednisone and sodium bicarbonate, and follow-up occurred with nephrology and oncology. Discharge medications included sodium bicarbonate.

The patient, a male, 21 years old, presented with dull, spasmodic abdominal pain for 7 days, localized at the right iliac fossa (RIF), worsening with movement, cough, and straining. The pain was accompanied by nausea, decreased appetite, and vomiting, without other symptoms like bowel or urinary issues. Medications were started during admission, and a gangrenous omental mass was detected during a laparoscopic procedure, which was surgically excised. Histopathology confirmed omental torsion, and the postoperative course was uneventful, with the patient discharged without complications. Follow-up is recommended, and discharge instructions advise avoiding strenuous activities and attending primary care follow-up.

A 39-year-old male presented with low back pain, right hip pain, and bilateral foot pain, followed by one-year progression to enlarging plantar soft masses in the right hallux. Initial lab results showed normal calcium but low phosphorus and elevated alkaline phosphatase, with FGF23 levels significantly elevated (indicating TIO). Tumor resection confirmed FGF23 overproduction, leading to a dramatic decrease in serum FGF23 and resolution of pain. Post-surgery, his symptoms improved, and follow-up appointments are recommended.

Discharge Summary:  
Patient information: Name N/A, Age 31, Gender Female, Medical Record Number N/A.  
Hospital course: Admitted to neurosurgery for a 5-month right occipital mass. Physical exam revealed a mass in the upper margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Head CT scan confirmed a 3×5 cm lesion with vascular components and a "wool mass." Further DSA showed an AVM, recommended for surgical removal. Post-op pathology confirmed IH with thrombolytic recanalization, leading to successful recovery. Follow-up results (1 year and 2 years) show partial residual IH without symptoms and no enlargement. Diagnosis: IH accompanied by thrombolytic recanalization. Course and outcome: Good recovery, one-year residual IH, and two-year no enlargement. Recommendation: Radiation therapy (refused).

Discharge Summary:  
A 24-year-old woman (admission 09/30/2006, discharge 10/04/2006) with myalgia, leukocytosis, neutrophilia, and monocytosis was discharged on 10/04/2006 with follow-up. She had elevated C-reactive protein, ESR, and creatine kinase, marked muscle tenderness, and a biopsy confirmed multifocal myonecrosis. Prescribed medications, diet, rest, and symptom reporting were followed.

The patient presented with shortness of breath, lower extremity edema, and flu-like symptoms. Initial treatment for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) was discontinued, and further investigation revealed a cardiac etiology. Diagnosed with a methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) infection, bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) with severe aortic regurgitation, and an ascending aortic aneurysm. Open-heart surgery with aortic valve replacement (AVR), ascending aortoplasty, and coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) were performed. Post-surgery, the patient recovered well with resolution of fever and bacteremia, and was discharged home on home health.

Discharge Summary:  
76-year-old male patient discharged on [insert date], with no medical history noted. The procedure involved dissection of an upper limb, identifying a Kaplan anastomosis from the dorsal ulnar nerve, which supplied synovial membranes, abductor of the fifth finger, and skin. The nerve merged with the ulnar trunk before bifurcation. This case differs from prior literature in the nerve union location. No further intervention required; patient discharged in good condition, advised follow-up with primary care physician.  

Signed, [Doctor's Name]

The patient, male, 3 years old, was admitted to the emergency unit for a 4-day history of fever and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Diagnosed with Listeria monocytogenes meningitis, intravenous amoxicillin and amikacin were prescribed, along with phenobarbitone for seizure control. Discharged after 3-week treatment with no fever or seizures. Follow-up included immunoglobulin therapy (initiated due to financial constraints) and vaccines (protein-conjugated pneumococcal and Haemophilus, prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole). Gait improved, and at 6-month follow-up, the patient was walking normally with no neurologic deficits. Parents were advised to monitor for recurrence and seek medical attention. Final diagnosis confirmed as Listeria monocytogenes meningitis.

A 37-year-old Caucasian-Italian female patient admitted in September 2006 with depressive mood, anxiety, psychosomatic symptoms, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and bulimic disorder was diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder according to DSM-IV criteria. She was treated with atypical antipsychotics, antidepressants, benzodiazepines, and psychotherapeutic interventions. Pharmacological therapy included atypical antipsychotics (ariprazine and topiramate), which improved mood and socio-relational functioning. She received psychological support to develop autonomy and ego functions. At discharge, her psychopathology was reduced, and she discontinued hypoglycemic treatment. Discharge diagnosis included Borderline Personality Disorder, Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, and Bulimic Disorder. Discharge medications were discontinued, and discharge instructions included continuing psychotherapy, maintaining a healthy diet, and adhering to dental follow-ups.

Discharge Summary:  
Admitted on [date], Discharged on [date], with a length of stay of [number of days]. Patient: [patient name],DOB: [date of birth], Sex: Male, Race: Caucasian.  

Medical History:  
- Enlarging crusting lesion on the anterior chest wall.  
- Palpable right and left pre-clavicular lymphadenopathy.  
- Lymph node–positive stage MCC with squamous cell carcinoma.  
- Mildly elevated lipase.  
- Metastases to pancreas and peripancreatic lymph nodes.  
- Completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy.

- Adjuvant radiation therapy initiated after multidisciplinary tumor board discussion.  
- New upper abdominal discomfort after RT, found pancreatic metastases.  
- Complete resolution of pancreatic masses and lymphadenopathy.  
- Passed away due to sudden cardiac arrest at home 1 month post-chemotherapy and 5 months post-diagnosis of pancreatic metastases.  

Follow-up: None as patient passed away.  
Primary Care Physician: None as patient passed away.  
Specialist(s): Oncologist.  
Dictated By: [clinician name], Date: [date of discharge summary].

The patient, diagnosed with a neck mass of papillary thyroid carcinoma, underwent a total thyroidectomy and adjuvant radioiodine therapy. Subsequent recurrence and metastasis were treated with radioiodine, stereotactic radiosurgery, surgical resection, and sorafenib. Due to the absence of second-line agents, she was enrolled in a phase II trial for entrectinib, which was successfully tested. The test revealed an EZR-ROS1 fusion, and she was treated with entrectinib. During treatment, she experienced muscle weakness and balance issues requiring dose reductions, with the lower dose tolerated. Discharge confirmed a stable condition with a partial response as per RECIST, resolving periaortic nodules and hypermetabolic liver metastases. Nontarget lesions in the left eighth rib and brain remained stable, and ongoing monitoring is recommended for long-term follow-up.

A 45-year-old woman with systemic symptoms of fever, weight loss, and malaise was referred to the hospital for a diagnosis of a violaceous plaques-associated disorder. She presented with multiple small violaceous plaques on her forehead, chest, abdomen, back, and extremities, along with a 37.1°C body temperature and painful lymph nodes. A skin biopsy revealed infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells, excluding malignant lymphoma, and no malignancy was detected. Discharge summary indicates she was treated with topical steroids and phototherapy, responded well to medication, and is now observed for follow-up. The disorder remains undiagnosed at this time, with a prognosis to be determined based on further diagnostic testing.

The patient, a 35-year-old male, was admitted with multiple injuries including abrasions over the right thigh, a lacerated wound over the right hand, and a deep perforated right eye injury. A CT scan was performed, revealing a globe rupture with a prolapsed and profusely bleeding ciliary body. Emergency evisceration was performed, and the patient was discharged after 2 weeks with follow-up care advised.

A 68-year-old man with aortic insufficiency and ascending aort dilatation was admitted to the emergency department presenting with exertional dyspnea and coughing. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 100/50 mmHg, heart rate of 80 beats/min, and a 3/6 diastolic decrescendo murmur. Chest X-ray showed increased cardiothoracic index and prominent aortic arch, with normal ECG findings. Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed severe aortic regurgitation, dilated ascending aorta (5.27 cm), and intimal dissection. Left ventricular ejection fraction was normal. The patient was immediately scheduled for surgery but died after a sudden cardiopulmonary arrest and CPR.

The patient, a 53-year-old woman with a history of pulmonary emphysema and recurrent pneumothorax, presented with fever, bilateral calf pain, and a cutaneous eruption in her lower extremities. She was treated for a pulmonary infection with Cefpodoxime two weeks prior. Admission blood tests showed elevated CRP, ferritin, and albumin levels, along with a right-sided apical lesion on chest CT and post-bronchoscopy sputum positive for Staphylococcus aureus. Diagnosed with leukocytoclastic vasculitis (HSP) consistent with IgA staining and confirmed by skin biopsy, and secondary findings of a pulmonary infection (Staphylococcus aureus and Mycobacterium xenopi), she was treated with Colchicine, then Methylprednisolone, and antibiotics. Follow-up showed improvement, no recurrence, and no renal disease.

A 64-year-old female cook with persistent right anterolateral thigh numbness and burning was diagnosed with meralgia paresthetica. She had a history of minor back trauma and asthma, managed with pregabalin 75-mg nocte and naproxen 275-mg twice daily. Nerve conduction studies and MRI confirmed the condition, revealing mild focal swelling in the right LFCN. Follow-up showed complete paraesthesia resolution without further treatment.
